title: Process Injection: Dynamic-link Library Injection
summary: This sub-technique is injection of a dynamic-link library into another live process, where a dynamic-link library, or DLL, is a module of code that Windows loads on demand. The classic form has the injector allocate memory in the target process, write the path of the library there, and then start a remote thread whose entry point makes the loader load that library, so the module appears inside the victim process and its code runs in that context. Reflective loading removes the on-disk path from the equation by writing a self-mapping image and performing the loader's work manually in memory, which defeats file-based inspection but produces private executable memory with no backing module. A related trick loads a legitimate signed library into the remote process and then overwrites the start address of its entry point, so the resulting activity is associated with a trusted file even though the bytes running are not the ones the vendor shipped. The strongest telemetry is behavioural rather than static: a thread created in a process other than the caller, an image load in a process that has no legitimate reason to load that library, executable private memory, and the original process creation event for the injector, which often shows a script interpreter or an unusual parent.

beginner.definition: A dynamic-link library is a file of code that Windows programs can load when they need it. This sub-technique is when an attacker forces another running program to load such a file. Their code then runs inside that program. It is part of the Process Injection parent technique. The difference is the payload type. Here the attacker brings a whole library file, or a copy of one held only in memory.
beginner.whyItMatters: The code then runs under a program your security tools already trust. Examples include a browser or a system process. Rules that allow those programs may allow the attacker too. It can also grant access to whatever that process can read, including data and privileged services. Finding it means looking at behaviour and memory rather than file names.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a target process, often one that is already running and trusted.
They reserve space inside that process and write a reference to their library, or a whole image, into it.
They start a thread in the target so the library is loaded there instead of in their own process.
A stealthier version loads the library only in memory, so no file on disk explains the code that runs.
Another version loads a signed library and then overwrites where its code begins, hiding behind a trusted file.
The injected code inherits the target's permissions, network access and readable memory.
beginner.example: Picture a secure office where visitors must sign in at reception. Instead of signing in, someone hides inside a delivery van that is already allowed through the gate. The gate log shows the van, not the person, and the guards wave it past as usual. Once inside, the person can walk into any room the van's driver may enter. Nothing in the visitor book explains how they got in.
takeaways: A trusted process can host code that did not come from its own files.
Cross-process thread creation and image loads are the events worth alerting on.
In memory libraries leave no disk file, so memory evidence matters.

objectives: Define a dynamic-link library and explain how Windows normally loads one.
Describe the classic cross-process loading behaviour and the remote thread it depends on.
Explain how in memory loading and entry point overwriting defeat file and signature checks.
Identify the process, thread, image load and memory telemetry that reveals this injection.
Explain how the injected code inherits the permissions and data access of the host process.
